keyVerseText: I say unto you, Though he will not rise and give him, because he is his friend, yet because of his importunity he will rise and give him as many as he needeth.
rootMeaning: The term ἀναίδεια (anaídeia) is formed from the negative particle Α and αἰδώς, which relates to a sense of reverence or shame. Literally, it conveys a state of being without shame or reverence, thus emphasizing shamelessness or impudence. This root meaning enriches the common English gloss of 'importunity' by highlighting an underlying boldness or lack of proper respect that compels persistence.
usageInScripture: This word appears only once in the New Testament, specifically in Luke 11:8, where it is translated as 'importunity.' The consistent translation as importunity suggests a focus on persistent, even bold, insistence. The lexical background also connects it to shamelessness, indicating that the persistence described is not merely polite asking but a kind of relentless boldness or shameless persistence.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding ἀναίδεια as shameless persistence deepens our grasp of prayer and faith in Scripture. It reveals that God welcomes not just polite requests but persistent, bold pleas that refuse to give up. This challenges believers to approach God with confidence, knowing that such importunity is not a mark of disrespect but of trust in His goodness. It also contrasts with attitudes of shame or hesitation, encouraging believers to overcome spiritual timidity by embracing a fearless boldness grounded in reverence for God.
keyVerseReflection: In Luke 11:8, Jesus illustrates that even a reluctant friend will respond to a request because of the petitioner’s importunity—this persistent, shameless asking. The word ἀναίδεια here highlights the power of determined prayer, showing that persistence can move the heart to generosity. It encourages believers to pray boldly and persistently, trusting that God honors such faith-filled importunity.
